Africa Clockwise

By: Annalise Lubbe | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We follow the Sampson family who circumvented Africa for 6 years in a big green truck using only vegetable oil.

Unique Selling Point:
A Cape Town family became the first people to cross Africa without petrol or diesel; a journey of over 47 000km crossing 29 African countries in a 1978 Mercedes using only vegetable oil.

Summary:
Mark Sampson is a South African comedian/climate change activist. In 2013 he, his wife Sam and their two young children, Ruby and Zola set out in the Big Green Truck, a 41 year old Mercedes 911 converted to run on vegetable oil, to make the first carbon neutral circumnavigation of the African continent. They expected the entire journey to take two years and finish before the kids hit high-school. In 2017 they had just finished driving up the West coast, 23000km through 20 countries, breaking down 15 times. This year they finished the journey, six and a half years, 47000km and 38 countries later. They broke down 27 times, got delayed 14 months behind closed borders in Liberia during the Ebola pandemic, and sometimes waited months to gather enough waste oil donations from hotels to fill up with fuel (this was how they ran the truck, showcasing an eco-friendly way of disposing of waste oil).

The idea of the trip was to show people (including their kids) how to live without thousands of possessions, and to ring an alarm bell about climate change. They say “In 2013 we thought we were going to be teaching our kids how to cope with extremes of weather and less water so they could pass resilience lessons on to their kids – we didn’t think they would be dealing with climate emergency in their lifetimes.”


Further information:
It was a summer day in 2013 from the sleepy village of Noordhoek when Mark, Sam, Zola and Rubi closed the doors of their new mobile home and put foot heading for the open road. Their destination? Africa!

They have worked for months preparing for this journey turning the inside of a rather big truck into a fully fledged home: complete with two sleeping areas, a shower and toilet, a kitchen and even a workspace where the children can be home schooled. Zola was only 6 and Rubi 11.

They used their savings from Mark’s comedy shows where he created awareness about climate change and living green and tossed all comforts out of the window to ensure they could survive off as little as possible living off the grid and eco-friendly. Sam tossed her job as a Managing Director of a company to spend every minute of the day with her children and together the family will experience the true meaning of ‘living’.

Kitted with solar power panels on the roof for electricity, they could run a fridge, the shower, the pumps and run LED lights.

They chose the name Africa Clockwise as they knew they were going up the west coast of Africa and back down the east coast and most importantly it is representative of the clock ticking and every second we are closer to climate change becoming a reality.

Their travels took them on life journey where they learnt the true meaning of friendship and kind people that opened their hearts and homes to the Sampson family. On one occasion they stayed in a convent whilst waiting for their truck to be repaired by a local mechanic who brought in his family to help fix the ‘big truck’.

They narrowly escaped the Ebola virus and had to leave Liberia until it was safe to go back. The Guinness World Records agreed to let them resume their attempt to beat the record for the longest distance travelled on alternative fuel once it was safe to go back to Liberia.

They crossed many rivers, lakes, mountains, on roads that were sometimes non-existent. But the longest and toughest road was from Boke in Guinea to the Guinea Bissau border. They were far from a town or repair shop but luckily found a handy man with a blowtorch who was happy to show his homegrown skills and once again the family was on their way.

The visuals: There are plenty of video footage and photos taken of their trip and many different experiences. The interviews will be done at the Getaway show where they will be exhibiting their big green truck kitted out with all the element that made it function off the grid.

Script:


Script: Africa Clockwise

V/O Meet the Sampson family: Mark and his wife Sam and their two teenage children, Ruby and Zola. They are at an outdoor show near Cape Town to create awareness about climate change. They have driven 47 000km through Africa in their green truck fuelled by recycled vegetable oil.

Mark: You start on diesel but we drive all day on vegetable oil and at the end of the day you flush it with diesel again. So everything is eco-friendly. We are doing it for climate change awareness.

V/O Mark is a stand-up comedian and has performed his shows on climate change in theatres and festivals across South Africa.

Up audio

Mark Sampson: Ten years ago I was doing a show about climate change and that research can be pretty depressing. And If thought I am frustrated, what can I do? I have got a big mouth, let’s see if I can get some awareness for the effects of climate change in Africa, get in the truck, run it on cooking oil, make it a carbon neutral vehicle and also show my kids a better value system.

Sam Pearce: You know in our family we have a very clear sense of “you have to seize the day”. I have a chronic illness. I don’t have infermous amount of energy any more than the planet
We felt the time pressure growing, clockwise because we need to wise up and take cognisance. But we don’t have time.

V/O Sam is a writer. She has suffered from myalgic encephalomyelitis or chronic fatigue syndrome since her early twenties. So planning to travel through Africa with a bed on board was not so much a “brave choice” as a practical solution to her deteriorating health.

Sam Pearce: We said the year Mark turns 40 we are going to set off and then he got to 40 and we realised we had not started. So it is like, ok you've got to take that first step.

V/O They found a 1978 Mercedes Benz truck, modified the diesel engine to run on recycled waste vegetable oil and, with the help of some carpenters, turned the inside into a fully functional mobile home. By going off the grid and living in a truck, they would cut their expenses to a quarter. Rental income from their house in Noordhoek would be used to cover their living costs.

Sam Pearce: Welcome to the big green truck. Here is the master bedroom and here is the en-suite.

Up sound: “{So tall our power is suploied by this victron monitor”.

V/O Clean drinking water is a scarce commodity in some parts of Africa. So Mark installed an onboard water purification system.

UP sound: So this is your water in here.

Macfarlane Moleli: So Mark what is this contraption?

Mark Samspon: It is an oil filter system. Basically when you get it is dirty and burnt and when you finish filtering it it looks like new oil again. So we use it in the engine and not in people’s stomachs because people all over Africa are getting stomach cancer.

V/O When cooking oil is repeatedly re-heated it becomes carcinogenic and could cause cancer. Street vendors across Africa use reheated oil which is hazardous to their health.

Mark Sampson: So it is not just about alternative energy and a different way of thinking about recycling and using energy, is a good health initiative.

V/O It took the family three years to prepare for the trip. In July 2013, they said goodbye to Cape Town. The plan was to travel up the west coast of Africa, cross briefly into Europe to avoid the politically unstable Algeria and Libya, and then drive back from Egypt down the east coast of Africa. Ruby was eleven and Zola, nine, at the time.

Macfarlane Moleli: Zola what were you thinking, what were you expecting?

Zola Sampson: Two years around Africa being away from school. I was afraid because I was going to be away from my friends but I was excited.

Ruby Sampson: I loved being in the truck more than what I loved living at home. I felt really safe in the truck. All and all it was the best experience of my life and I would not change it for anything.

Macfarlane Moleli: In which of these countries did you start seeing the immediate effect of climate change, and what we are doing to destroy mother nature?

Sam Pearce: We drove into Namibia and they were having such a terrible drought and the herdsman, we stopped to talk to them we saw these trees with all these cardboards hanging from them and we asked them if it was some sort of recycling plant and they said no that is feed for the cattle. So they soak the cardboard in brine and they feed that to the cattle so the cattle think they are eating something. When we got into Angola the drought was worse. We could not get water anywhere.

V/O Ruby discovered children like her living in absolute poverty. It is estimated that hundreds of millions of people in Africa do not have access to safe drinking water due to poverty.

Ruby Sampson: The first bad thing I truly became aware of was climate change. Seeing the drought in Namibia but not only the bad also the good of how they are dealing with it.

V/O Further up the coast, more signs of extreme weather were evident. Many roads were simply washed away. The Sampsons frequently got stuck in their big green truck; often, it would break down.

Up sound

V/O Once back on the road, finding vegetable oil was essential. Fortunately, running on reused cooking oil meant hotels and restaurants in cities everywhere had ample to give away. And in return for their generosity, Mark would put on a magic show to entertain the children.

Up sound

Mark Sampson: The kindness has been incredible. This has been, “ubuntu”, “umoja”, “on est ensemble”, the language of inclusion.

V/O Mark and Zola are both keen surfers. They took advantage of the best surf in Africa while travelling along the coastal route.

Macfarlane Moleli: Where were some of the biggest waves that you caught?

Zola Sampson: Biggest was Liberia and Senegal. I love big waves. Big waves are my companion.

V/O Tropical diseases are rife in Africa. The whole family contracted malaria and typhoid and recovered. What they didn’t foresee was being stuck in the middle of the Ebola virus epidemic when it broke out in Monrovia, the capital of Liberia. But they managed to evacuate just in time.

Macfarlane Moleli: Were you ever in danger?

Mark Sampson: Nobody ever fired a shot. In 6 years we had a couple of small incidents and we always talked our way out of it.

V/O There were many highlights: For Ruby, it was seeing the pyramids in Egypt; for Zola, swimming with a turtle in the Red Sea; and for the whole family, Christmas in Nigeria during the Calabar Carnival.

Up music: dancing girls

V/O By now, the family had been on the road for nearly six years. They were on the east coast driving towards Mozambique when one of the worst weather-related disasters in the southern hemisphere was imminent.

Sam Pearce: We broke down terribly in Malawi. Looking back we were so lucky because if he hadn't we would have been on the coast in northern Mozambique in the period that those two cyclones hit within 5.5 weeks and no two cyclones of that magnitude have ever hit Mozambique within that time period.

V/O They recognised this disaster as just one more symptom of the effects of climate change.

Sam Pearce: You know when we left we genuinely thought that we were going to prepare our children so that they could prepare their children for what was coming. But we did not think that we would be seeing the effects of climate emergency in their lifetimes.

V/O After six and a half years, the Sampson family has returned home. Zola is preparing for a career at sea studying at a maritime centre; Ruby is pouring her passion for the environment into working with a climate activist group; Sam is writing a book about her travels and how she has coped with her chronic illness against all odds; and Mark is planning new shows about climate change to educate the youth on what everyone can do to make a difference.

_______________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________

Promo one:
When the Sampson family left Cape Town six years ago to explore Africa, little did they know that a deadly disease and a catastrophic cyclone would cross their paths on this epic adventure.

Promo two:
A Cape Town family drove 47 000 km through Africa in a truck powered by waste vegetable oil in their quest to see if a future without fossil-fuelled luxuries was possible.

Promo three:
They fled from the deadly Ebola virus, narrowly escaped two cyclones, and drove 47 000 km across the African continent in a truck fuelled by waste vegetable oil to learn about climate change.

Sam Pearce: We drove into Namibia and they were having such a terrible drought and the herdsman, we stopped to talk to them we saw these trees with all these cardboards hanging from them and we asked them if it was some sort of recycling plant and they said no that is feed for the cattle. So they soak the cardboard in brine and they feed that to the cattle so the cattle think they are eating something. When we got into Angola the drought was worse. We could not get water anywhere. V/O Ruby discovered children like her living in absolute poverty. It is estimated that hundreds of millions of people in Africa do not have access to safe drinking water due to poverty. Ruby Sampson: The first bad thing I truly became aware of was climate change. Seeing the drought in Namibia but not only the bad also the good of how they are dealing with it. V/O Further up the coast, more signs of extreme weather were evident. Many roads were simply washed away. The Sampsons frequently got stuck in their big green truck; often, it would break down. Up sound V/O Once back on the road, finding vegetable oil was essential. Fortunately, running on reused cooking oil meant hotels and restaurants in cities everywhere had ample to give away. And in return for their generosity, Mark would put on a magic show to entertain the children. Up sound Mark Sampson: The kindness has been incredible. This has been, “ubuntu”, “umoja”, “on est ensemble”, the language of inclusion. V/O Mark and Zola are both keen surfers. They took advantage of the best surf in Africa while travelling along the coastal route. Macfarlane Moleli: Where were some of the biggest waves that you caught? Zola Sampson: Biggest was Liberia and Senegal. I love big waves. Big waves are my companion. V/O Tropical diseases are rife in Africa. The whole family contracted malaria and typhoid and recovered. What they didn’t foresee was being stuck in the middle of the Ebola virus epidemic when it broke out in Monrovia, the capital of Liberia. But they managed to evacuate just in time. Macfarlane Moleli: Were you ever in danger? Mark Sampson: Nobody ever fired a shot. In 6 years we had a couple of small incidents and we always talked our way out of it. V/O There were many highlights: For Ruby, it was seeing the pyramids in Egypt; for Zola, swimming with a turtle in the Red Sea; and for the whole family, Christmas in Nigeria during the Calabar Carnival. Up music: dancing girls V/O By now, the family had been on the road for nearly six years. They were on the east coast driving towards Mozambique when one of the worst weather-related disasters in the southern hemisphere was imminent. Sam Pearce: We broke down terribly in Malawi. Looking back we were so lucky because if he hadn't we would have been on the coast in northern Mozambique in the period that those two cyclones hit within 5.5 weeks and no two cyclones of that magnitude have ever hit Mozambique within that time period. V/O They recognised this disaster as just one more symptom of the effects of climate change. Sam Pearce: You know when we left we genuinely thought that we were going to prepare our children so that they could prepare their children for what was coming. But we did not think that we would be seeing the effects of climate emergency in their lifetimes. V/O After six and a half years, the Sampson family has returned home. Zola is preparing for a career at sea studying at a maritime centre; Ruby is pouring her passion for the environment into working with a climate activist group; Sam is writing a book about her travels and how she has coped with her chronic illness against all odds; and Mark is planning new shows about climate change to educate the youth on what everyone can do to make a difference. _______________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________ Promo one: When the Sampson family left Cape Town six years ago to explore Africa, little did they know that a deadly disease and a catastrophic cyclone would cross their paths on this epic adventure. Promo two: A Cape Town family drove 47 000 km through Africa in a truck powered by waste vegetable oil in their quest to see if a future without fossil-fuelled luxuries was possible. Promo three: They fled from the deadly Ebola virus, narrowly escaped two cyclones, and drove 47 000 km across the African continent in a truck fuelled by waste vegetable oil to learn about climate change. __________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________ Invoicing Back references from Insert ID in Invoice: Title Author Last Updated Invoice for Africa Clockwise (5640) Annalise Lubbe 23 March 2020

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): We follow the Sampson family who circumvented Africa for 6 years in a big green truck using only vegetable oil.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: A Cape Town family became the first people to cross Africa without petrol or diesel; a journey of over 47 000km crossing 29 African countries in a 1978 Mercedes using only vegetable oil.
metadata.Summary: Mark Sampson is a South African comedian/climate change activist. In 2013 he, his wife Sam and their two young children, Ruby and Zola set out in the Big Green Truck, a 41 year old Mercedes 911 converted to run on vegetable oil, to make the first carbon neutral circumnavigation of the African continent. They expected the entire journey to take two years and finish before the kids hit high-school. In 2017 they had just finished driving up the West coast, 23000km through 20 countries, breaking down 15 times. This year they finished the journey, six and a half years, 47000km and 38 countries later. They broke down 27 times, got delayed 14 months behind closed borders in Liberia during the Ebola pandemic, and sometimes waited months to gather enough waste oil donations from hotels to fill up with fuel (this was how they ran the truck, showcasing an eco-friendly way of disposing of waste oil). The idea of the trip was to show people (including their kids) how to live without thousands of possessions, and to ring an alarm bell about climate change. They say “In 2013 we thought we were going to be teaching our kids how to cope with extremes of weather and less water so they could pass resilience lessons on to their kids – we didn’t think they would be dealing with climate emergency in their lifetimes.”
metadata.Further information: It was a summer day in 2013 from the sleepy village of Noordhoek when Mark, Sam, Zola and Rubi closed the doors of their new mobile home and put foot heading for the open road. Their destination? Africa! They have worked for months preparing for this journey turning the inside of a rather big truck into a fully fledged home: complete with two sleeping areas, a shower and toilet, a kitchen and even a workspace where the children can be home schooled. Zola was only 6 and Rubi 11. They used their savings from Mark’s comedy shows where he created awareness about climate change and living green and tossed all comforts out of the window to ensure they could survive off as little as possible living off the grid and eco-friendly. Sam tossed her job as a Managing Director of a company to spend every minute of the day with her children and together the family will experience the true meaning of ‘living’. Kitted with solar power panels on the roof for electricity, they could run a fridge, the shower, the pumps and run LED lights. They chose the name Africa Clockwise as they knew they were going up the west coast of Africa and back down the east coast and most importantly it is representative of the clock ticking and every second we are closer to climate change becoming a reality. Their travels took them on life journey where they learnt the true meaning of friendship and kind people that opened their hearts and homes to the Sampson family. On one occasion they stayed in a convent whilst waiting for their truck to be repaired by a local mechanic who brought in his family to help fix the ‘big truck’. They narrowly escaped the Ebola virus and had to leave Liberia until it was safe to go back. The Guinness World Records agreed to let them resume their attempt to beat the record for the longest distance travelled on alternative fuel once it was safe to go back to Liberia. They crossed many rivers, lakes, mountains, on roads that were sometimes non-existent. But the longest and toughest road was from Boke in Guinea to the Guinea Bissau border. They were far from a town or repair shop but luckily found a handy man with a blowtorch who was happy to show his homegrown skills and once again the family was on their way. The visuals: There are plenty of video footage and photos taken of their trip and many different experiences. The interviews will be done at the Getaway show where they will be exhibiting their big green truck kitted out with all the element that made it function off the grid.
